name: Attention is a filter
head: Attention works like a filter: we're aware of what it lets through
receipt: Source: Simons, 'Failures of Awareness: The Case of Inattentional Blindness', Noba Project

vo_marked: Start with attention. [beat] Your eyes take in far more than your mind can handle. [beat] So attention acts like a *filter*. It picks what matters for the task in front of you... and quietly drops the rest. [beat] It's more ruthless than my email's spam folder, which, honestly, is saying a lot about my... [beat] anyway. [pause] That's useful. It's how you read in a noisy café. [beat] But it has a cost.

Start with attention. Your eyes take in far more than your mind can handle. So attention acts like a filter. It picks what matters for the task in front of you... and quietly drops the rest. It's more ruthless than my email's spam folder, which, honestly, is saying a lot about my... anyway.

name: The gorilla experiment
head: Inattentional blindness: missing the unexpected while focused on something else
receipt: Source: Simons, Noba Project; Simons and Chabris (1999), as described there
visual: Definition layout. Left: term 'Inattentional blindness' and Noba definition 'The surprising failure to notice an unexpected object or event when attention is focused on something else.' [S4]. Right: simple schematic of the 1999 experiment as three numbered steps (no video stills): '1 Count passes by the team in white' / '2 A person in a gorilla suit walks through' / '3 Asked: did you notice anything unusual?'. Result strip: 'About half missed the gorilla' [S3].
media: ANIM; Right side, captions built in; Original diagram of the 1999 experiment: players passing, gorilla walking through (Done)
vo_marked: That cost has a name: *inattentional blindness*. [beat] Missing something unexpected because your attention is busy elsewhere.
[pause] The famous test came in the late nineties. Viewers counted passes between players in white shirts.
[beat] Midway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the middle of the scene, thumped their chest, and walked off.
[pause] About half the viewers never saw it.
vo_plain:
That cost has a name: inattentional blindness. Missing something unexpected because your attention is busy elsewhere.

The famous test came in the late nineties. Viewers counted passes between players in white shirts. Midway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the middle of the scene, thumped their chest, and walked off.

About half the viewers never saw it.

name: What makes you miss
head: You miss more when the task is harder or the surprise blends in
receipt: Source: Simons, Noba Project (citing Simons and Chabris, 1999; Most et al., 2001)
visual: Driver tree. Root 'Chance of missing the unexpected' (navy). Branch 1: 'A harder task' with example 'Keeping separate counts of bounce passes and aerial passes made viewers less likely to notice the gorilla' [S6]. Branch 2: 'It resembles what you're ignoring' with example 'Viewers counting the team in white missed the dark gorilla more than those counting the team in black' [S7]. Bottom note: 'Even unique items get missed: about 30% failed to see a bright red cross crossing the screen for five seconds' [S8].
media: VIDEO; full screen under tint; basketball one-on-one (Mixkit #44468)
vo_marked: Two things make it worse. [beat] First, a harder task. [beat] When viewers kept separate counts of bounce passes and air passes, they were even less likely to see the gorilla.
[pause] Second, if the surprise looks like the stuff you're ignoring. [beat] People counting the team in white missed the dark gorilla more often.
[pause] Even a bright red cross, the only coloured thing on screen, went unseen by about thirty percent of people.
vo_plain:
Two things make it worse. First, a harder task. When viewers kept separate counts of bounce passes and air passes, they were even less likely to see the gorilla.

Second, if the surprise looks like the stuff you're ignoring. People counting the team in white missed the dark gorilla more often.

Even a bright red cross, the only coloured thing on screen, went unseen by about thirty percent of people.
